Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation before being relied on in production.

The reference material consulted while preparing these pages is listed in the section bibliography.

Checked against R 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) on 2026-10-20; R 4.6.2 is scheduled for 2026-10-29. A package is only as usable as its documentation: every exported function, dataset and class needs a help page, R CMD check reports the ones that do not have one, and a long-form guide (a vignette) is what turns a set of functions into something a newcomer can start from. R’s own documentation format is Rd, a LaTeX-like markup language that R converts to plain text, HTML, LaTeX and runnable example code, and that nobody writes by hand any more if they can avoid it: roxygen2 generates the Rd files from comments written next to the code. This page covers the whole chain. It starts with Rd itself and the base-R tools that parse, convert and check it, goes on to roxygen2 (its tags, its markdown, the way it documents data and S3, S4, R6 and S7 classes, how it reuses text), and then to vignettes (knitr and R Markdown, and Quarto), pkgdown websites, the inst/CITATION file and NEWS.md. The tools that ran for real are base R with its tools and utils packages, roxygen2 8.1.1, devtools 2.5.2, usethis 3.2.2, knitr 1.52, rmarkdown 2.32 (with the Pandoc that rmarkdown finds), pkgdown 2.2.1 and withr 3.0.3; S7 0.2.2 and R6 2.6.1 are only documented, not used; the Quarto command-line program 1.10.19 rendered one file; and the default linters of lintr 3.4.0 were used only to check the scripts. The quarto R package (the vignette engine for Quarto) is not installed in the image, so what it adds is described and not run, and the same holds for the doclisting package, the GitHub Actions workflow of a pkgdown site and every command that needs a GitHub account. The image also has no TeX installation, so the conversion to PDF is shown failing and the conversions that work without TeX are shown instead.

Every example is a script that was run with Rscript on R 4.6.1 with warnings printed as they happen (options(warn = 1)), and the lines that start with #> are what it printed. The scripts also pass the default lintr linters. The names books, loans and the book() constructor belong to the running library-shelf scenario described on the section index. The shelf package shown here was created, documented, tested, built and checked for real with these tools, and its files are shown as the tools wrote them: the man/*.Rd files, the NAMESPACE and the DESCRIPTION fields were written by roxygen2 and usethis, and vignettes/shelf.Rmd, inst/CITATION and NEWS.md are the files of the package. Scripts that change the package (devtools::document(), R CMD build, R CMD check) worked on a copy of it. Paths are shortened to ~/shelf (the directory of the package) and ~ (the directory that holds it), the platform lines at the top of an R CMD check log are left out, and so are timings and temporary directories. Quotation marks in messages are the typographic quotes that R prints in a UTF-8 locale. Where a script writes an Rd file or a throwaway package, it writes it to a temporary directory, builds a small package there and prints the generated file: the file text on the page is what roxygen2 wrote.

This page continues the package pages. Creating Packages builds the shelf package and explains DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE and the R CMD commands, Testing with testthat tests it and Publishing to CRAN submits it. How to read the documentation that this page teaches you to write is in Getting Help and Documentation.

The documentation a package carries

A package has several kinds of documentation, written in different formats, found in different places of the source tree and read with different functions. The table lists them; the sections of this page take them in this order.

Where in the source What it is Written with Read with

man/*.Rd

one help page (topic) per Rd file

roxygen2 comments, or Rd by hand

help(), ?, example(), help(package = "shelf")

DESCRIPTION

Title, Description, Authors@R, URL, BugReports

by hand

packageDescription(), the package page help(package = )

vignettes/ (rendered into inst/doc by R CMD build)

long-form guides

R Markdown with knitr, Quarto, Sweave

vignette(), browseVignettes()

inst/CITATION

how to cite the package

bibentry() calls

citation()

NEWS.md (or inst/NEWS.Rd)

what changed in each version

Markdown by hand

news()

man/figures/, man/macros/

images and user-defined macros used by the Rd files

by hand

the help pages that use them

_pkgdown.yml, README.md

the configuration and the home page of a pkgdown website (not part of the installed package)

by hand

a web browser

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package subdirectories

The shelf package has most of them. The script lists the files of the source tree that carry documentation. NAMESPACE is in the list because roxygen2 writes it from the same comments as the Rd files (the @export and @importFrom tags), and R/data.R because the datasets are documented in a file of their own.

# The files of the package that carry documentation, relative to its root.
files <- list.files(recursive = TRUE, all.files = TRUE)
pattern <- paste0(
  "^(DESCRIPTION|NAMESPACE|NEWS[.]md|[.]Rbuildignore|",
  "man/|vignettes/|inst/|R/data[.]R|data-raw/)"
)
grep(pattern, files, value = TRUE)
#>  [1] ".Rbuildignore"          "data-raw/books.csv"     "data-raw/books.R"
#>  [4] "data-raw/loans.csv"     "DESCRIPTION"            "inst/CITATION"
#>  [7] "man/book-methods.Rd"    "man/book.Rd"            "man/books.Rd"
#> [10] "man/clean_books.Rd"     "man/loan_summary.Rd"    "man/loans_per_month.Rd"
#> [13] "man/loans.Rd"           "man/normalise_isbn.Rd"  "man/overdue_loans.Rd"
#> [16] "NAMESPACE"              "NEWS.md"                "R/data.R"
#> [19] "vignettes/.gitignore"   "vignettes/shelf.Rmd"

Source: R documentation: list.files

R CMD check looks at all of it. These are the steps of the real check of the shelf tarball that concern documentation, from the log of a check with --as-cran and the remote part of the incoming checks switched off (the check itself is the subject of Publishing to CRAN); each one is explained where its subject comes up below.

* checking Rd files ... OK
* checking Rd metadata ... OK
* checking Rd line widths ... OK
* checking Rd cross-references ... OK
* checking for missing documentation entries ... OK
* checking for code/documentation mismatches ... OK
* checking Rd \usage sections ... OK
* checking Rd contents ... OK
* checking for unstated dependencies in examples ... OK
* checking contents of ‘data’ directory ... OK
* checking data for non-ASCII characters ... OK
* checking LazyData ... OK
* checking data for ASCII and uncompressed saves ... OK
* checking R/sysdata.rda ... OK
* checking installed files from ‘inst/doc’ ... OK
* checking files in ‘vignettes’ ... OK
* checking examples ... OK
* checking for unstated dependencies in vignettes ... OK
* checking package vignettes ... OK
* checking re-building of vignette outputs ... OK

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

Rd: the documentation format of R

R objects are documented in files written in the R documentation format, Rd. Writing R Extensions describes it as a simple markup language, much of which closely resembles (La)TeX, that can be processed into a variety of formats including LaTeX, HTML and plain text. The R distribution contains more than 1400 such files, one or more per function of the base and recommended packages, and every help page you have read in R was produced from one. When a package is installed, its Rd files are parsed and stored in the library in a binary form (the help directory of the installed package), and help() renders them on demand: as text in a terminal, as HTML in the browser. That design is the reason that the same source gives a page in the console, a page on the CRAN site, a chapter of the PDF reference manual and the examples that example() runs.

The anatomy of a file

An Rd file has three parts. The header is mandatory and gives the name of the file, the topics documented, a title, a short description and the usage of the objects documented. The body (arguments, value, details, examples and so on) gives the rest, and an optional footer carries keywords. The sections are macros that start with a backslash and take their arguments in braces, and they can appear in any order. Unless a section is allowed to repeat, only the first occurrence of a standard section is kept, with a warning. This is the file that roxygen2 wrote for normalise_isbn() and is_valid_isbn13(), which share one page:

% Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand
% Please edit documentation in R/isbn.R
\name{normalise_isbn}
\alias{normalise_isbn}
\alias{is_valid_isbn13}
\title{Normalise and validate ISBN-13 strings}
\usage{
normalise_isbn(x)

is_valid_isbn13(x)
}
\arguments{
\item{x}{A character vector of ISBNs; \code{NA} and empty strings are allowed.}
}
\value{
\code{normalise_isbn()} returns a character vector of the same length;
\code{is_valid_isbn13()} a logical vector of the same length, \code{FALSE} for
\code{NA} and for the empty string.
}
\description{
\code{normalise_isbn()} drops everything except digits and \code{X} and upper-cases
the result, so \code{"978-0-00-100010-0"} and \code{"9780001000100"} compare equal.
\code{is_valid_isbn13()} checks that a (normalised) string has 13 digits and a
correct check digit: the digits are multiplied alternately by 1 and 3 and
the sum must be divisible by 10.
}
\examples{
normalise_isbn("978-0-00-100010-0")
is_valid_isbn13(c("978-0-00-100010-0", "9780001000101", "", NA))
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Rd format

The first two lines are Rd comments (a percent sign starts a comment that runs to the end of the line) and tell a human not to edit the file. Then come the sections, in the order roxygen2 writes them. The most used ones, with the kind of text each takes, are in the table. Writing R Extensions distinguishes four kinds of input: LaTeX-like text with markup macros, verbatim text where nothing but the comment marker is interpreted, R-like text for code with some embedded macros, and a rare verbatim variant, used in the first argument of \eqn, \deqn, \figure and \newcommand, in which the comment marker need not be escaped.

Section What it holds Input

\name{topic}

the unique name of the Rd object, normally the base name of the file; one per file; no markup, only printable ASCII; it may not contain !, | or @

verbatim

\alias{topic}

a topic that help() can find; one per topic documented; an alias need not be an object’s name (format.book is an alias of the page book-methods)

verbatim

\title{...}

the title; capitalised, no final period, at most about 65 characters; exactly one

LaTeX-like

\description{...}

a short paragraph on what the objects do; mandatory except in package overview pages

LaTeX-like

\usage{...}

the synopsis, which has to match the code exactly so that the checks can compare them; S3 methods are written \method{generic}{class}(args), S4 methods \S4method{generic}{class}(args)

R-like

\arguments{...}

one \item{name}{description} per argument, or several names separated by commas

LaTeX-like

\value{...}

what the function returns; a list can be described with \item{name}{description} entries

LaTeX-like

\details{...}

the detailed description

LaTeX-like

\note{...}, \references{...}, \author{...}, \seealso{...}

notes, literature (with \doi{}, \url{}), the authors, pointers to related topics

LaTeX-like

\examples{...}

code that is shown and run by example() and R CMD check

R-like

\keyword{key}, \concept{term}

index entries; the standard keywords are listed in the KEYWORDS file of R; the keyword internal hides a page from the topic indices

verbatim

\format{...}, \source{...}, \docType{...}

for data sets: the structure, the origin, and the type of the object (data, package, class, methods)

LaTeX-like

\section{Title}{...}, \subsection{Title}{...}

a section of your own, and a subsection inside a section (more than three levels do not format well); extra sections are always printed before \note, \seealso and the examples, whatever their position in the source

LaTeX-like

\encoding{UTF-8}

the encoding, on a line by itself, when the file has non-ASCII characters

verbatim

Source: Writing R Extensions: Documenting functions

An Rd file therefore has the same skeleton as every help page you have read in R: the title, Description, Usage, Arguments, Details, Value, Note, References, See Also and Examples. Writing R Extensions also states a rule for the title: capitalised, without a final period, no more than about 65 characters. R 4.4.0 made tools::checkRd() report titles and section names that end in a period; R CMD check ignores that finding unless the environment variable _R_CHECK_RD_CHECKRD_MINLEVEL_ is set to -5 or smaller (the NEWS entry is in the version notes below).

Looking at the parse tree

Rd is parsed by tools::parse_Rd(), which returns a list of class Rd in which every element carries its macro in the attribute Rd_tag. That is the structure that every converter and every check below walks. The script parses man/book.Rd (written by roxygen2 from R/book.R) and looks at the top level: the two comment lines, then \name, three \alias entries and the sections.

# Parse man/book.Rd (written by roxygen2) and look at the parse tree.
rd <- tools::parse_Rd("man/book.Rd")
class(rd)
#> [1] "Rd"
tags <- vapply(rd, \(x) attr(x, "Rd_tag"), character(1))
tags[tags != "TEXT"]
#>  [1] "COMMENT"       "COMMENT"       "\\name"        "\\alias"
#>  [5] "\\alias"       "\\alias"       "\\title"       "\\usage"
#>  [9] "\\arguments"   "\\value"       "\\description" "\\examples"
#> [13] "\\seealso"     "\\concept"
length(rd)
#> [1] 28

# The text of an element: its leaves pasted together.
rd_text <- \(x) paste(vapply(x, as.character, character(1)), collapse = "")

# The \alias entries are what help() searches.
vapply(rd[tags == "\\alias"], rd_text, character(1))
#> [1] "book"          "new_book"      "validate_book"

# The title and the concept index entry as plain text.
rd_text(rd[[which(tags == "\\title")]])
#> [1] "The book class"
rd_text(rd[[which(tags == "\\concept")]])
#> [1] "book class"

# The parts of the usage section, as the parser sees them.
usage <- rd[[which(tags == "\\usage")]]
attr(usage, "Rd_tag")
#> [1] "\\usage"
attr(usage[[2L]], "Rd_tag")
#> [1] "RCODE"

Source: R documentation: parse_Rd

The three aliases of the page book are book, new_book and validate_book: help("new_book") finds this page because of that alias, not because of the name of the file. The same holds for format.book and the page book-methods, which the section on help lookup below shows. The technical description of the parser is the document "Parsing Rd files" on the R developer site (Parsing Rd files).

Rd markup in one file

The macros for marking text, building lists and tables, linking, writing mathematics and running code are the part of Rd that people look up. This is a hand-written Rd file that uses most of them, rendered as text with tools::Rd2txt(). The script writes the Rd text to a temporary file with a raw string, so that the page shows the Rd as it is typed, and then converts it, running the three stages of evaluation of \Sexpr (explained below). The option underline_titles = FALSE only keeps the backspace-based underlining of the section titles, which a terminal shows and a page cannot, out of the output.

# A hand-written Rd file that uses most of the markup macros, rendered as text.
rd_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "loan_rules.Rd")
writeLines(r"---(\newcommand{\isbn}{\code{ISBN-13}}
\name{loan_rules}
\alias{loan_rules}
\title{Loan Rules of the Shelf Library}
\description{
  The loan period is \code{getOption("shelf.loan_days")} days; set it
  with \code{\link{options}}, or with the environment variable
  \env{SHELF_LOAN_DAYS} in \file{.Renviron}. See \pkg{shelf},
  \emph{emphasis}, \strong{strong text} and \sQuote{single} or
  \dQuote{double} quotes; \verb{x[[1]]} is shown verbatim.
  A book is identified by its \isbn{} (see \doi{10.32614/R.manuals}).
}
\details{
  \itemize{
    \item A loan is overdue after \eqn{d > 21} days.
    \item Members may hold \eqn{n \le 5}{n <= 5} loans.
  }
  \enumerate{
    \item Take the book out.
    \item Return it.
  }
  \describe{
    \item{late}{returned after the loan period.}
    \item{out}{not returned yet.}
  }
  \tabular{lrr}{
    genre \tab loans \tab overdue \cr
    Fiction \tab 12 \tab 6 \cr
    Poetry \tab 4 \tab 1
  }
  The rate is \deqn{r = \frac{o}{n}}{r = o / n}
  See \url{https://example.com/shelf} and
  \href{https://example.com/shelf/rules}{the rules}.
  This text is for the console: \ifelse{text}{plain text}{rich text}.
}
\section{Evaluated when the page is built}{
  The page has \Sexpr[stage=build]{length(letters)} letters in its
  alphabet and is rendered with \Sexpr[stage=render]{R.version$language}.
}
\examples{
x <- 1:3
sum(x)
\dontrun{stop("never run")}
\donttest{max(x)}
\dontshow{stopifnot(is.numeric(x))}
}
\keyword{documentation}
)---", rd_file)
tools::Rd2txt(
  rd_file,
  stages = c("build", "install", "render"),
  options = list(underline_titles = FALSE)
)
#> Loan Rules of the Shelf Library
#>
#> Description:
#>
#>      The loan period is ‘getOption("shelf.loan_days")’ days; set it
#>      with ‘options’, or with the environment variable ‘SHELF_LOAN_DAYS’
#>      in ‘.Renviron’. See ‘shelf’, _emphasis_, *strong text* and
#>      ‘single’ or “double” quotes; x[[1]] is shown verbatim.  A book is
#>      identified by its ‘ISBN-13’ (see doi:10.32614/R.manuals
#>      <https://doi.org/10.32614/R.manuals>).
#>
#> Details:
#>
#>         • A loan is overdue after d > 21 days.
#>
#>         • Members may hold n <= 5 loans.
#>
#>        1. Take the book out.
#>
#>        2. Return it.
#>
#>      late
#>           returned after the loan period.
#>
#>      out
#>           not returned yet.
#>
#>        genre    loans  overdue
#>        Fiction     12        6
#>        Poetry       4        1
#>
#>      The rate is
#>
#>                                   r = o / n
#>
#>      See <https://example.com/shelf> and the rules.  This text is for
#>      the console: plain text.
#>
#> Evaluated when the page is built:
#>
#>      The page has 26 letters in its alphabet and is rendered with R.
#>
#> Examples:
#>
#>      x <- 1:3
#>      sum(x)
#>      ## Not run: stop("never run")
#>      max(x)
#>

# The default is stages = "render": a build-stage macro is then left as written.
small <- file.path(tempdir(), "small.Rd")
writeLines(r"---(\name{small}
\alias{small}
\title{Small}
\description{
  Built: \Sexpr[stage=build]{length(letters)};
  rendered: \Sexpr[stage=render]{R.version$language}.
}
)---", small)
tools::Rd2txt(small, options = list(underline_titles = FALSE))
#> Small
#>
#> Description:
#>
#>      Built: \Sexpr[stage=build]{length(letters)}; rendered: R.
#>

Source: Writing R Extensions: Marking text

Every macro on the page has a purpose, and the plain-text conversion shows what happens to each one. The marking macros are logical, not physical: \code{} says "a piece of R code or the name of an R object" and each output format chooses the typography (typewriter font in HTML and PDF, typographic quotes in text). \emph{} and \strong{} emphasise (the text conversion uses underscores and asterisks), \sQuote{} and \dQuote{} quote without hard-wiring the quotation marks, \pkg{} names a package, \file{} a file, \env{} an environment variable, \option{} a command-line option, \command{} a command, \email{} an address, \var{} a metasyntactic variable, \kbd{} keyboard input, \samp{} a literal sequence of characters, \dfn{} a defining use of a term, \cite{} a reference without a link, \acronym{} and \abbr{} abbreviations. \verb{} and \preformatted{} keep their text exactly, and \url{} and \href{url}{text} write links to the web (the first argument of both is verbatim, with percent signs and braces escaped by a backslash). Two macros are built in for text that cannot be written plainly: \R for the name of the language and \ldots or \dots for an ellipsis; both should be followed by {} unless a space follows.

Lists and tables have three list macros and one table macro. \itemize and \enumerate take \item followed by a space and the text, with no braces; \describe takes \item{label}{body} with two arguments, exactly like the entries of \arguments and \value; \tabular{lrr}{...} takes the alignment of each column (l, r or c) and then lines separated by \cr with fields separated by \tab. There must be the same number of fields on each line as columns, and there is no white space between \tabular and its first argument. Mathematics uses \eqn{latex}{ascii} for inline formulas and \deqn{latex}{ascii} for displayed ones: the first argument is typeset by KaTeX or MathJax in HTML help (from R 4.2.0) and by LaTeX in the PDF manual, the second is what the plain-text help shows, and a single argument serves for both when the LaTeX source is readable as text (the text converter also knows the relations \le, \ge and \ne). In the output above \eqn{d > 21} has the one-argument form and \eqn{n \le 5}{n <= 5} has two.

Three macros decide what an output format sees. \if{format}{text} and \ifelse{format}{text}{alternate} select by output format (example, html, latex or text; TRUE matches all formats); \out{literal} writes its text unescaped and is used inside \if{html}{} to emit raw HTML; and a block between a line #ifdef windows (or #ifdef unix, or #ifndef with either) and a line #endif is included or excluded for one operating system before the page is processed. Platform-specific Rd files can also live in man/unix and man/windows subdirectories. In the console conversion above, \ifelse{text}{plain text}{rich text} produced "plain text".

Source: Writing R Extensions: Conditional text

Links and cross-references

\link{foo}, usually inside \code{}, links to the help page that has foo as an alias, in this or any installed package; whitespace is stripped when an alias is stored but not when a link target is looked up. There are four forms, and the second matters for S3 and S4 classes, which have no function of their own to link to.

Form Meaning

\link{foo}

link to the topic foo, displayed as foo

\link[=dest]{name}

link to the topic dest, displayed as name; the way to refer to an S3 class (\link[=terms.object]{terms}) or an S4 class (\link[=abc-class]{abc}); since R 4.5.0 the displayed text may contain markup such as \eqn{}

\link[pkg]{foo}, \link[pkg:bar]{foo}

link to the topic foo (or bar) in package pkg; the package must be in Depends, Imports, Suggests or Enhances; since R 4.1.0 this is a link to the topic (before that, to a file foo.html)

\linkS4class{abc}, \linkS4methods{xyz}

shorthand for the S4 class abc and for the methods of the generic xyz; the second is new in R 4.6.0

Source: Writing R Extensions: Cross-references

A link to a topic that does not exist is not an error when the page is converted; it is reported by R CMD check ("checking Rd cross-references"), and roxygen2 reports it while documenting. Both messages appear in the roxygen2 sections below. \concept{term} adds an index term for help.search() and ??, but a \concept cannot be the target of a link: link targets are aliases. Vignettes can be linked from help pages with relative URLs of the form ../doc/file.html, and a help page can link to a vignette of another package with ../../pkg/doc/file.html.

Examples: what is shown, what is run

The \examples section is both documentation and a test: its code is shown on the page, run by example() and run by R CMD check, so an example must be executable on any machine, without Internet access, without interaction and without writing outside a temporary directory. Four macros control that. They appear in the output of the previous script: the code in \dontrun{} is shown (as a comment, ## Not run:) but never run; \donttest{} code is shown and run by example() but, by default, not by R CMD check; \dontshow{} code is run but not shown (it used to be called \testonly, which is still accepted); and \dontdiff{} (new in R 4.4.0) marks code whose output is ignored when the check output is compared with a saved reference output.

R 4.0.0 changed what \donttest means for a CRAN submission: R CMD check --as-cran now runs the \donttest examples too, instead of telling the tester to run them (setting _R_CHECK_DONTTEST_EXAMPLES_ to a false value turns that off during development). So \donttest no longer hides slow or fragile examples from the CRAN checks; it only hides them from a plain R CMD check. The documentation recommends it only for code that may fail in circumstances that are hard to test for, with a comment that explains why. Code that needs a service, a key or a program that may be missing is better guarded by a condition, which is what the roxygen2 tag @examplesIf below writes. Examples that read from stdin, such as scan(), cannot run, because example() uses source(). Data for examples comes from random numbers or from the standard data sets (data()).

Source: Writing R Extensions: Documenting functions, the examples section

Dynamic pages: \Sexpr and \RdOpts

\Sexpr[options]{code} evaluates R code inside an Rd file and inserts the result. The options follow Sweave’s format: eval (default TRUE), echo (default FALSE), keep.source (default TRUE), results (text, the default, applies as.character() to the value; verbatim shows the printed value; rd parses the result as Rd and inserts it, which is how aliases can be computed; hide), strip.white and stage. stage is the important one: stage=build runs when the source tarball is built, stage=install (the default) when the package is installed from source, and stage=render each time the page is displayed. The order is always build, then the #ifdef conditionals, then install, then render, and code runs once in each stage, so a \Sexpr[results=rd] can output a \Sexpr for a later stage but not for the current or an earlier one. \RdOpts{} sets new defaults for the \Sexpr that follow it. The file above has a build-stage and a render-stage \Sexpr in one sentence. The first conversion ran all three stages with stages = c("build", "install", "render") and printed "26 letters" and "R"; the second, at the end of the script, ran a small file with the default stages = "render" and left the build-stage macro exactly as written, because for a package that stage is over by the time the page is rendered. In a package the build stage is the way to compute something once, when the tarball is made (the R 4.6.0 macros for bibliographic citations are built that way), the install stage fits text that depends on the installation, and the render stage text that must be current every time the page is shown. Since R 4.6.0 the error message of a failed \Sexpr includes the call of the original condition, and warnings include the Rd source location.

User-defined macros, encoding and figures

\newcommand and \renewcommand define macros inside an Rd file. They take two verbatim arguments, the name of the new macro with its backslash and its definition, and the definition may use placeholders #1 to #4; the number of arguments is the highest placeholder seen, and the arguments are substituted as text before the result is parsed. \newcommand refuses a name that is already defined, \renewcommand replaces one, built-in macros included. The file above defined \isbn as \code{ISBN-13} in its first line. R ships a set of system macros in the file share/Rd/macros/system.Rd that are available in every Rd file: \doi{} for a digital object identifier, \CRANpkg{} for a package on CRAN, \sspace for a space after a period that does not end a sentence, \packageTitle{} and its relatives (\packageDescription, \packageAuthor, \packageMaintainer, \packageDESCRIPTION, \packageIndices) that read the fields of DESCRIPTION when the package is built, and, new in R 4.6.0, \manual{name}{node} to refer to a section of one of the R manuals. Macros that several pages of a package share go into an Rd file in man/macros, which is installed into help/macros, and a package can use the macros of another by naming it in the RdMacros field of DESCRIPTION.

An Rd file with a character outside ASCII needs an \encoding{} line, unless DESCRIPTION declares Encoding: UTF-8, which shelf does; the file is converted to UTF-8 before parsing and UTF-8 is the preferred encoding. The manual advises avoiding non-ASCII characters in Rd files wherever possible, and also the symbols <, >, $, ^, &, |, @, ~ and * outside verbatim environments, because some fonts used for PDF manuals do not render them; tools::showNonASCIIfile() finds the offending bytes. For one word that must be written differently where an encoding is unavailable, \enc{Jöreskog}{Joreskog} gives the encoded and the ASCII form.

Figures for help pages go into man/figures, and \figure{file}{alternate text} includes one: the file types .jpg, .jpeg, .pdf, .png and .svg in that directory are copied to the help/figures directory of the installed package. The text conversion shows the alternate text instead. PDF figures show in the PDF manual and not in a browser, and SVG the other way round, which is why roxygen2 has the option restrict_image_formats for images added through markdown.

Source: Writing R Extensions: User-defined macros

Special characters

Four characters need care in Rd. A percent sign starts a comment in every kind of text and has to be written \%, except in the rare verbatim variant. A backslash is written \\. A brace that is not balanced has to be escaped, and all of %, {, } and \ must be escaped in LaTeX-like text. In R-like text (the usage and examples sections) quoted strings are handled differently: braces inside a string do not need escapes. The mistake that costs most time is the percent sign, because the rest of the line, including a closing brace, disappears into the comment. tools::checkRd() is the tool that finds these mistakes, and the next script feeds it six small broken files and shows what it reports for each. It writes every file to a temporary directory and removes that directory from the messages.

# tools::checkRd() on small broken Rd files; each case shows what R reports.
check_rd <- \(label, lines) {
  f <- file.path(tempdir(), "broken.Rd")
  writeLines(lines, f)
  res <- NULL
  msg <- capture.output(
    res <- tryCatch(tools::checkRd(f), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e)),
    type = "message"
  )
  out <- capture.output(print(res))
  # Keep the temporary directory out of the messages.
  cat(label, ":\n", sep = "")
  cat(sub(paste0(tempdir(), "/"), "", c(msg, out), fixed = TRUE), sep = "\n")
}

check_rd("no title", c("\\name{a}", "\\alias{a}", "\\usage{a()}"))
#> no title:
#> [1] "broken.Rd: Sections \\title, and \\name must exist and be unique in Rd files"

check_rd("unclosed brace", c(
  "\\name{a}", "\\alias{a}", "\\title{T}",
  "\\description{An unclosed {brace.", "}"
))
#> unclosed brace:
#> prepare_Rd: broken.Rd:6: unexpected END_OF_INPUT '
#> '
#> checkRd: (-1) broken.Rd:4-5: Lost braces; missing escapes or markup?
#>      4 | \description{An unclosed {brace.
#>        |                          ^

check_rd("macro without its backslash", c(
  "\\name{a}", "\\alias{a}", "\\title{T}",
  "\\description{Use code{x} here.}"
))
#> macro without its backslash:
#> checkRd: (-1) broken.Rd:4: Lost braces
#>      4 | \description{Use code{x} here.}
#>        |                      ^

check_rd("misspelt macro", c(
  "\\name{a}", "\\alias{a}", "\\title{T}",
  "\\description{Use \\codee{x} here.}"
))
#> misspelt macro:
#> prepare_Rd: broken.Rd:4: unknown macro '\codee'

check_rd("unescaped percent sign", c(
  "\\name{a}", "\\alias{a}", "\\title{T}",
  "\\description{It is 50% done.}", "\\examples{x <- 1}"
))
#> unescaped percent sign:
#> prepare_Rd: broken.Rd:5: unexpected section header '\examples'
#> prepare_Rd: broken.Rd:6: unexpected END_OF_INPUT '
#> '
#> checkRd: (-1) broken.Rd:5: Lost braces; missing escapes or markup?
#>      5 | \examples{x <- 1}
#>        |          ^

check_rd("title ending in a period, item with two arguments", c(
  "\\name{a}", "\\alias{a}", "\\title{A title.}", "\\description{Text.}",
  "\\details{\\itemize{\\item{x}{y}}}"
))
#> title ending in a period, item with two arguments:
#> checkRd: (-5) broken.Rd:3: \title should not end in a period
#> checkRd: (-3) broken.Rd:5: Lost braces
#>      5 | \details{\itemize{\item{x}{y}}}
#>        |                        ^
#> checkRd: (-1) broken.Rd:5: Lost braces in \itemize; meant \describe ?

Source: R documentation: checkRd

The messages are worth learning to read. A file without a \title fails the structural check at once. An unclosed brace gives a parser message ("unexpected END_OF_INPUT") followed by "Lost braces" with the offending line and a caret. A macro without its backslash (code{x} for \code{x}) is not an error for the parser, since code{x} is just text followed by a braced group, and is reported as "Lost braces". A misspelt macro is "unknown macro" at parse time. The unescaped percent sign swallowed the closing brace of \description and the \examples section that followed, so the parser reports an "unexpected section header" and then the lost braces. The last file has two further findings: the number in parentheses is the level of the message (-5 is the lowest, for style), and the title ending in a period only appears at that low level; "Lost braces in \itemize; meant \describe ?" is the message for \item{x}{y} used inside \itemize, where \item takes no braces. In a package, R CMD check runs these checks for every file in man in the step "checking Rd files".

Writing Rd by hand with prompt()

prompt() writes an Rd skeleton for a function or data frame that you then edit, with comments (%%) that tell you what to write where. It is the older, manual route: the skeleton is correct for the arguments that exist on the day it is written, and you keep it in step by hand afterwards. promptData(), promptPackage() (and, from the methods package, promptClass() and promptMethods()) do the same for data, packages and S4 classes and methods, and package.skeleton() writes a whole package skeleton with such files, as Creating Packages shows. The script runs prompt() on normalise_isbn() of the installed shelf and prints the start of the file:

# prompt() writes an Rd skeleton for a function, to be edited by hand.
library(shelf)
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
file <- file.path(tempdir(), "normalise_isbn.Rd")
invisible(capture.output(
  prompt(normalise_isbn, filename = file),
  type = "message"
))
head(readLines(file), 16)
#>  [1] "\\name{normalise_isbn}"
#>  [2] "\\alias{normalise_isbn}"
#>  [3] "%- Also NEED an '\\alias' for EACH other topic documented here."
#>  [4] "\\title{"
#>  [5] "A Capitalized Title (ideally limited to 65 characters)"
#>  [6] "}"
#>  [7] "\\description{"
#>  [8] "%%  ~~ A concise (1-5 lines) description of what the function does. ~~"
#>  [9] "}"
#> [10] "\\usage{"
#> [11] "normalise_isbn(x)"
#> [12] "}"
#> [13] "%- maybe also 'usage' for other objects documented here."
#> [14] "\\arguments{"
#> [15] "  \\item{x}{"
#> [16] "%%     ~~Describe \\code{x} here~~"

Source: R documentation: prompt

Everything between the \description, \usage and \arguments braces is placeholder text. Leaving the placeholders in is a classic CRAN rejection ("A Capitalized Title (ideally limited to 65 characters)" shipped as a title), and the reason most packages that document by hand run R CMD check before every commit.

Converting Rd

The conversions of an Rd file are functions of the tools package, and the R CMD commands wrap them. The input is a file, the result is text, HTML, LaTeX or R code, and none of the conversions needs anything but R except the PDF.

Plain text: Rd2txt

tools::Rd2txt() is what help("book") runs when it shows a page in a terminal. The result of converting man/book.Rd is the page below: the title, the sections in the order of the help system, the markup replaced by typography (\code{} by single typographic quotes) and the usage written in the form the function has. The script is run in a copy of the package, in which man/book.Rd is relative to the package root.

# Render man/book.Rd as plain text, the way help("book") shows it in a terminal.
tools::Rd2txt("man/book.Rd", options = list(underline_titles = FALSE))
#> The 'book' class
#>
#> Description:
#>
#>      ‘book()’ is the user-facing constructor of the ‘book’ class: it
#>      trims the text fields, normalises the ISBN with
#>      ‘normalise_isbn()’, coerces ‘year’ and ‘pages’ to integer and
#>      validates the result. ‘new_book()’ is the low-level constructor
#>      that only checks types, and ‘validate_book()’ checks the values;
#>      both are exported so that other packages can extend the class.
#>
#> Usage:
#>
#>      book(
#>        title,
#>        author = NA_character_,
#>        isbn = NA_character_,
#>        year = NA_integer_,
#>        genre = NA_character_,
#>        pages = NA_integer_
#>      )
#>
#>      new_book(
#>        title = character(),
#>        author = character(),
#>        isbn = character(),
#>        year = integer(),
#>        genre = character(),
#>        pages = integer()
#>      )
#>
#>      validate_book(x)
#>
#> Arguments:
#>
#>    title: Title of the book (a single string).
#>
#>   author: Author (a single string, or ‘NA’).
#>
#>     isbn: ISBN-13, hyphenated or bare (a single string, or ‘NA’).
#>
#>     year: Publication year (a single number, or ‘NA’).
#>
#>    genre: Genre (a single string, or ‘NA’).
#>
#>    pages: Number of pages (a single number, or ‘NA’).
#>
#>        x: A ‘book’ object.
#>
#> Value:
#>
#>      An object of class ‘book’: a list with the six fields above, each
#>      of length one.
#>
#> See Also:
#>
#>      Other book class: ‘book-methods’
#>
#> Examples:
#>
#>      b <- book("  the quiet streets ", "Mara Quill", "978-0-00-100010-0", 2019,
#>                "Fiction ", 214)
#>      b
#>      summary(b)
#>      unclass(b)
#>

Source: R documentation: Rd2txt, Rd2HTML, Rd2latex and Rd2ex

HTML, examples and LaTeX

tools::Rd2HTML() writes the HTML that help() shows in the browser and that CRAN and pkgdown show on the web, tools::Rd2ex() writes the examples as an R script and tools::Rd2latex() writes the LaTeX that R CMD Rd2pdf feeds to pdflatex. The script converts the same file with each one into temporary files and shows the headings of the HTML page, the extracted examples, and the first lines of the LaTeX. The header that Rd2ex() writes records the page name, the title and the aliases, which is why running a package’s examples gives traceable output.

# The same Rd file through the other converters, written to temporary files.
html <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
tools::Rd2HTML("man/book.Rd", out = html, package = "shelf")
lines <- readLines(html)
# The title line of the page and the headings of its sections.
grep("R Documentation|^<h[23]", lines, value = TRUE)
#> [1] "<table style=\"width: 100%;\"><tr><td>book {shelf}</td><td style=\"text-align: right;\">R Documentation</td></tr></table>"
#> [2] "<h2>The <code>book</code> class</h2>"
#> [3] "<h3>Description</h3>"
#> [4] "<h3>Usage</h3>"
#> [5] "<h3>Arguments</h3>"
#> [6] "<h3>Value</h3>"
#> [7] "<h3>See Also</h3>"
#> [8] "<h3>Examples</h3>"

# Rd2ex() extracts the examples, with a header that records the page.
ex <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
tools::Rd2ex("man/book.Rd", out = ex)
cat(readLines(ex), sep = "\n")
#> ### Name: book
#> ### Title: The 'book' class
#> ### Aliases: book new_book validate_book
#>
#> ### ** Examples
#>
#> b <- book("  the quiet streets ", "Mara Quill", "978-0-00-100010-0", 2019,
#>           "Fiction ", 214)
#> b
#> summary(b)
#> unclass(b)
#>
#>
#>

# Rd2latex() writes the LaTeX that R CMD Rd2pdf feeds to pdflatex.
tex <- tempfile(fileext = ".tex")
tools::Rd2latex("man/book.Rd", out = tex)
head(readLines(tex), 6)
#> [1] "\\HeaderA{book}{The \\code{book} class}{book}"
#> [2] "\\aliasA{new\\_book}{book}{new.Rul.book}"
#> [3] "\\aliasA{validate\\_book}{book}{validate.Rul.book}"
#> [4] "\\keyword{book class}{book}"
#> [5] "%"
#> [6] "\\begin{Description}"

Source: R documentation: Rd2txt, Rd2HTML, Rd2latex and Rd2ex

R CMD Rdconv

R CMD Rdconv is the command-line interface to the text, HTML, LaTeX and example conversions of one Rd file. The option -t chooses the type (txt, html, latex or example), and R CMD Rdconv --help lists the rest. The command is run in the directory that holds shelf:

R CMD Rdconv -t example shelf/man/normalise_isbn.Rd
echo "exit status: $?"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Processing documentation files

### Name: normalise_isbn
### Title: Normalise and validate ISBN-13 strings
### Aliases: normalise_isbn is_valid_isbn13

### ** Examples

normalise_isbn("978-0-00-100010-0")
is_valid_isbn13(c("978-0-00-100010-0", "9780001000101", "", NA))



exit status: 0

Source: Writing R Extensions: Processing documentation files

The output is the example script of the page normalise_isbn, with the same header as Rd2ex() wrote above. Running the examples of an installed package is also what example(book) does, and the help-lookup section below shows it.

R CMD Rd2pdf and the PDF reference manual

R CMD Rd2pdf builds a PDF from Rd files, given either as files or as the path of a package, in which case it builds the reference manual of the whole package with the information of DESCRIPTION. It converts the Rd files to LaTeX and runs LaTeX on the result, so it needs a TeX installation with pdflatex. The image used for this page has none, so the attempt, run on the shelf package with --no-preview so that it would not try to open a viewer, fails. The failure message and the exit status are what R reports:

R CMD Rd2pdf --no-preview --output=shelf-manual.pdf shelf
echo "exit status: $?"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Processing documentation files

Hmm ... looks like a package
Converting Rd files to LaTeX
Creating pdf output from LaTeX ...
Warning in texi2dvi(file = file, pdf = TRUE, clean = clean, quiet = quiet,  :
  texi2dvi script/program not available, using emulation
Error in texi2dvi(file = file, pdf = TRUE, clean = clean, quiet = quiet,  :
  pdflatex is not available
Warning in texi2dvi(file = file, pdf = TRUE, clean = clean, quiet = quiet,  :
  texi2dvi script/program not available, using emulation
Error in texi2dvi(file = file, pdf = TRUE, clean = clean, quiet = quiet,  :
  pdflatex is not available
Error in running tools::texi2pdf()
exit status: 1

Source: R documentation: Rd2pdf

The first stage, "Converting Rd files to LaTeX", worked; the second, "Creating pdf output from LaTeX", did not, because tools::texi2pdf() looks for the texi2dvi program, falls back to an emulation, and the emulation needs pdflatex on the path ("pdflatex is not available"). It reports it twice because it tries twice. The manual R Installation and Administration states the requirement: building PDF vignettes and manuals needs a distribution of LaTeX with pdflatex. With a TeX distribution (TeX Live, MacTeX, MiKTeX or the smaller TinyTeX) the same command writes shelf-manual.pdf. The consequences for the rest of the work are simple. The conversions to text, HTML and examples need no TeX, and neither does anything else on this page; R CMD check builds the PDF manual as one of its steps and, without TeX, reports a WARNING and then an ERROR in the steps "checking PDF version of manual" (the real lines are in Publishing to CRAN), which is why every check of the shelf package on this page was run with --no-manual; and the HTML vignettes that this page builds need Pandoc and no TeX, while PDF vignettes need TeX. R 4.5.0 changed R CMD Rd2pdf so that the Rd.sty of the running R takes precedence over any other version in the TeX tree.

Source: R Installation and Administration: Essential and useful other programs under a Unix-alike

How help() finds a page

An installed package keeps its Rd files in a parsed form. The script looks at what the installation of the Rd files of shelf left in the library: the help directory with the topic index (aliases.rds maps every alias to the Rd file it came from, AnIndex is the index that help() reads, shelf.rdb and shelf.rdx hold the parsed pages), and the table Meta/Rd.rds from which help.search() and the package index are built.

# What the installation of the Rd files leaves in the library.
help_dir <- system.file("help", package = "shelf")
list.files(help_dir)
#> [1] "aliases.rds" "AnIndex"     "paths.rds"   "shelf.rdb"   "shelf.rdx"

# aliases.rds maps every \alias to the Rd file (the topic name) it came from.
aliases <- readRDS(file.path(help_dir, "aliases.rds"))
aliases[c("format.book", "is_valid_isbn13", "new_book", "clean_loans")]
#>      format.book  is_valid_isbn13         new_book      clean_loans
#>   "book-methods" "normalise_isbn"           "book"    "clean_books"

# Meta/Rd.rds is the table that help.search() and the HTML index are built from.
rd <- readRDS(system.file("Meta", "Rd.rds", package = "shelf"))
names(rd)
#> [1] "File"     "Name"     "Type"     "Title"    "Encoding" "Aliases"  "Concepts"
#> [8] "Keywords"
rd[, c("File", "Name", "Title")]
#>                 File            Name                                   Title
#> 1    book-methods.Rd    book-methods            Methods for the 'book' class
#> 2            book.Rd            book                        The 'book' class
#> 3           books.Rd           books                     The shelf catalogue
#> 4     clean_books.Rd     clean_books Clean the catalogue and the loans table
#> 5    loan_summary.Rd    loan_summary       Loans and overdue rates per genre
#> 6           loans.Rd           loans                         The shelf loans
#> 7 loans_per_month.Rd loans_per_month                         Loans per month
#> 8  normalise_isbn.Rd  normalise_isbn  Normalise and validate ISBN-13 strings
#> 9   overdue_loans.Rd   overdue_loans                           Overdue loans
rd$Aliases[[2L]]
#> [1] "book"          "new_book"      "validate_book"
rd$Concepts[[2L]]
#> [1] "book class"

Source: R documentation: help

The lookup functions use those files. help(package = "shelf") lists the topics of the package (its index), help("topic", package = ) finds a page by alias, ?? and help.search() look in titles, aliases, concepts and keywords, and example() runs the \examples of a page. The script shows each one, including what help() says about a topic that does not exist.

# How help() finds the page of an installed package.
library(shelf)
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days

# help(package =) lists the topics of the package: its index.
h <- help(package = "shelf")
class(h)
#> [1] "packageInfo"
cat(h$info[[2L]], sep = "\n")
#> book                    The 'book' class
#> book-methods            Methods for the 'book' class
#> books                   The shelf catalogue
#> clean_books             Clean the catalogue and the loans table
#> loan_summary            Loans and overdue rates per genre
#> loans                   The shelf loans
#> loans_per_month         Loans per month
#> normalise_isbn          Normalise and validate ISBN-13 strings
#> overdue_loans           Overdue loans

# A topic is an \alias. format.book is an alias of the page book-methods.
basename(help("book", package = "shelf"))
#> [1] "book"
basename(help("new_book", package = "shelf"))
#> [1] "book"
basename(help("format.book", package = "shelf"))
#> [1] "book-methods"
help("no_such_topic", package = "shelf")
#> No documentation for ‘no_such_topic’ in specified packages and libraries:
#> you could try ‘??no_such_topic’

# ?? and help.search() look in titles, aliases and concepts. Printing the
# result shows it in the pager; the table of matches is a data frame.
hs <- help.search("ISBN", package = "shelf")
class(hs)
#> [1] "hsearch"
hs$matches[, c("Topic", "Field", "Entry")]
#>            Topic Field                                  Entry
#> 1 normalise_isbn alias                         normalise_isbn
#> 2 normalise_isbn alias                        is_valid_isbn13
#> 3 normalise_isbn Title Normalise and validate ISBN-13 strings

# example() runs the \examples of the page.
example(book)
#>
#> book> b <- book("  the quiet streets ", "Mara Quill", "978-0-00-100010-0", 2019,
#> book+           "Fiction ", 214)
#>
#> book> b
#> <book> the quiet streets (Mara Quill, 2019)
#>
#> book> summary(b)
#> Book: the quiet streets
#> ISBN known: TRUE
#> Pages: 214
#>
#> book> unclass(b)
#> $title
#> [1] "the quiet streets"
#>
#> $author
#> [1] "Mara Quill"
#>
#> $isbn
#> [1] "9780001000100"
#>
#> $year
#> [1] 2019
#>
#> $genre
#> [1] "Fiction"
#>
#> $pages
#> [1] 214
#>

Source: R documentation: help.search

format.book and new_book are not pages of their own; they are aliases of the pages book-methods and book, which is why one Rd file can document a whole family. help.search("ISBN") found the page normalise_isbn three times, by the alias normalise_isbn, by the alias is_valid_isbn13 and by the word in the title. The listing of example(book) is what the \examples section of man/book.Rd did when run through source() with the book> prompt: \dontshow code would have run silently, and \dontrun code would have been shown as a comment.

roxygen2: Rd files from comments

Rd is a good format for a machine and a poor one to maintain: the usage section has to repeat the signature of the function exactly, every argument has to be described in a separate block, and each of these is far from the code that changes. roxygen2 moves the documentation into the R source, in special comments that start with #' and sit immediately above the object they document, and writes the Rd files, the NAMESPACE and the Collate field from them. The usage section is taken from the function itself, so it cannot disagree with the code, and the arguments, the exports and the documentation of a function are in one place. roxygen2 is a CRAN package (8.1.1 on 2026-10-08); the 8.0.0 release of 2026-05-01 is the one that requires R 4.1 and moved the package’s settings into Config/roxygen2/ fields of DESCRIPTION, as the section on DESCRIPTION below explains.

Blocks, tags and the first paragraphs

A block is a run of #' lines. The first paragraph is the title, the second is the description, and any further paragraph is the details, unless a tag says otherwise. A tag is a word that starts with @ at the start of a line, and everything up to the next tag belongs to it. The example below uses a throwaway package in a temporary directory, so that nothing but the generated files is involved: one function with a title, a description with markdown code and a link, a details paragraph with a list, a parameter tag that documents two parameters, a return value, an example, and the two namespace tags @importFrom and @export. The script runs roxygen2::roxygenise() and prints the Rd file and the NAMESPACE that came out.

# A throwaway package with one documented function, turned into Rd by roxygen2.
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "demo")
dir.create(file.path(pkg, "R"), recursive = TRUE)
writeLines(c(
  "Package: demo",
  "Title: A Demonstration",
  "Version: 0.0.1",
  "Description: Shows what roxygen2 writes.",
  "License: MIT",
  "Encoding: UTF-8",
  "Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE"
), file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION"))

writeLines(r"(#' Take a book out
#'
#' Records a loan of `book` to `member`. The loan is overdue after
#' `days` days. Summarise loan lengths with [stats::median()].
#'
#' The second paragraph is the *details* section. A list:
#' * one
#' * two
#'
#' @param book A book (a string).
#' @param member,days Name of the member and length of the loan.
#' @returns A list with the three inputs.
#' @examples
#' loan_book("Dune", "Ana")
#' @importFrom stats median
#' @export
loan_book <- function(book, member, days = 21L) {
  list(book = book, member = member, days = days)
}
)", file.path(pkg, "R", "loan.R"))

invisible(capture.output(roxygen2::roxygenise(pkg), type = "message"))
cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "man", "loan_book.Rd")), sep = "\n")
#> % Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand
#> % Please edit documentation in R/loan.R
#> \name{loan_book}
#> \alias{loan_book}
#> \title{Take a book out}
#> \usage{
#> loan_book(book, member, days = 21L)
#> }
#> \arguments{
#> \item{book}{A book (a string).}
#>
#> \item{member, days}{Name of the member and length of the loan.}
#> }
#> \value{
#> A list with the three inputs.
#> }
#> \description{
#> Records a loan of \code{book} to \code{member}. The loan is overdue after
#> \code{days} days. Summarise loan lengths with \code{\link[stats:median]{stats::median()}}.
#> }
#> \details{
#> The second paragraph is the \emph{details} section. A list:
#> \itemize{
#> \item one
#> \item two
#> }
#> }
#> \examples{
#> loan_book("Dune", "Ana")
#> }
cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "NAMESPACE")), sep = "\n")
#> # Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand
#>
#> export(loan_book)
#> importFrom(stats,median)

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Documenting functions

The mapping is the one to remember. The title went to \title, the first paragraph after it to \description, the second to \details. @param member,days became one \item{member, days} entry, because a tag can document several arguments with one text. @returns became \value. The \usage section was not written by hand: roxygen2 took it from the function. The markdown in the description was translated (`book` to \code{book}, [stats::median()] to a link to the median topic in stats, *details* to \emph, the list to \itemize), and the two namespace tags went to the NAMESPACE file, not to the Rd file: export(loan_book) and importFrom(stats,median). The tag @importFrom stats median is there only to show the directive; in a real package it sits in the block of a function that calls median().

What roxygenise() does

roxygen2::roxygenise() (spelt roxygenize() too) takes a package directory, loads the package code, parses the blocks and runs the roclets. A roclet is a processor of the parsed blocks that produces one kind of output: rd writes man/*.Rd, namespace writes NAMESPACE, collate writes the Collate field of DESCRIPTION from the @include tags. Those three run by default. By default the package is loaded with pkgload, and the code is evaluated, so that roxygen2 knows what a function, a dataset or a class looks like. devtools::document() is the usual front end: it calls roxygenise() and prints its progress. roxygen2::needs_roxygenize() (new in 8.0.0) answers cheaply whether the Rd files are older than their sources. Every file roxygen2 writes starts with the comment lines "Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand" and "Please edit documentation in R/book.R", and roxygen2 only rewrites files that carry that header. The script reads the settings of shelf as roxygen2 sees them.

# The options roxygen2 reads for the package, and where they come from.
read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", fields = c("Roxygen", "Config/roxygen2/version"))
#>      Roxygen                 Config/roxygen2/version
#> [1,] "list(markdown = TRUE)" "8.1.1"
opts <- roxygen2::load_options(".")
opts$roclets
#> [1] "collate"   "namespace" "rd"
opts$markdown
#> [1] TRUE
opts$load
#> [1] "pkgload"

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: load_options

A file that was not written by roxygen2 is left alone. This matters when you convert a package that has hand-written Rd files, and it is the message to know: the script puts a hand-written loan_book.Rd where roxygen2 wants to write one, and roxygen2 refuses to overwrite it, tells you why and leaves the file as it was. (The first two lines are the first-run message of roxygen2 8, which also sets the version field in DESCRIPTION.)

# roxygen2 does not overwrite an Rd file that it did not write itself.
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "demo")
dir.create(file.path(pkg, "R"), recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(file.path(pkg, "man"))
writeLines(c(
  "Package: demo",
  "Title: A Demonstration",
  "Version: 0.0.1",
  "Description: Shows what roxygen2 writes.",
  "License: MIT",
  "Encoding: UTF-8",
  "Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE"
), file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION"))
writeLines(c(
  "#' Take a book out",
  "#' @export",
  "loan_book <- function() 1"
), file.path(pkg, "R", "loan.R"))
writeLines(c(
  "\\name{loan_book}",
  "\\alias{loan_book}",
  "\\title{Written by hand}",
  "\\description{Not generated.}"
), file.path(pkg, "man", "loan_book.Rd"))

msg <- capture.output(roxygen2::roxygenise(pkg), type = "message")
sub("\\(<file://.*>\\)", "(man/loan_book.Rd)", msg)
#> [1] "First time using roxygen2. Upgrading automatically..."
#> [2] "ℹ Setting Config/roxygen2/version to \"8.1.1\""
#> [3] "ℹ Loading demo"
#> [4] "Writing 'NAMESPACE'"
#> [5] "✖ Skipping loan_book.Rd (man/loan_book.Rd)"
#> [6] "ℹ It already exists and was not generated by roxygen2."
cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "man", "loan_book.Rd")), sep = "\n")
#> \name{loan_book}
#> \alias{loan_book}
#> \title{Written by hand}
#> \description{Not generated.}

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: roxygenise

The first run and the second run of document()

The first time devtools::document() is run on a package whose blocks link to each other, roxygen2 warns: a link such as [normalise_isbn()] in the description of book() points to a topic whose Rd file does not exist yet, because it is written in the same run, after the link is checked. The second run finds the files and is clean. This is the real sequence on shelf, from a copy of the package in which man/ and NAMESPACE were deleted first, as after writing the R files and before documenting them. The script collects the messages of the first run into first, shows how many there are, the first nine, the lines that start with a cross, and the last ten, and then runs it again. The page shows both runs.

# Start from a package with no man/ and no NAMESPACE, as after use_r() only.
unlink(c("man", "NAMESPACE"), recursive = TRUE)
list.files()
#>  [1] "cran-comments.md" "data"             "data-raw"         "DESCRIPTION"
#>  [5] "inst"             "LICENSE"          "LICENSE.md"       "NEWS.md"
#>  [9] "R"                "tests"            "vignettes"

# First run: every [fn()] link to a topic that does not exist yet is reported.
# The messages are collected so that the listing can be shortened below.
first <- capture.output(devtools::document(), type = "message")
length(first)
#> [1] 83
head(first, 9)
#> [1] "ℹ Updating shelf documentation"
#> [2] "ℹ Loading shelf"
#> [3] "shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days"
#> [4] "✖ book.R:3: @description Could not resolve link to topic \"normalise_isbn\" in"
#> [5] "  the dependencies or base packages.."
#> [6] "ℹ If you haven't documented \"normalise_isbn\" yet, or just changed its name,"
#> [7] "  this is normal. Once \"normalise_isbn\" is documented, this warning goes away."
#> [8] "ℹ Make sure that the name of the topic is spelled correctly."
#> [9] "ℹ Always list the linked package as a dependency."
grep("^[✖]", first, value = TRUE)
#>  [1] "✖ book.R:3: @description Could not resolve link to topic \"normalise_isbn\" in"
#>  [2] "✖ clean.R:10: @param Could not resolve link to topic \"books\" in the"
#>  [3] "✖ clean.R:11: @param Could not resolve link to topic \"loans\" in the"
#>  [4] "✖ data.R:3: @description Could not resolve link to topic \"clean_books\" in the"
#>  [5] "✖ data.R:25: @description Could not resolve link to topic \"books\" in the"
#>  [6] "✖ data.R:25: @description Could not resolve link to topic \"clean_loans\" in the"
#>  [7] "✖ loans.R:8: @param Could not resolve link to topic \"loans\" in the dependencies"
#>  [8] "✖ loans.R:8: @param Could not resolve link to topic \"clean_loans\" in the"
#>  [9] "✖ loans.R:42: @description Could not resolve link to topic \"overdue_loans\" in"
#> [10] "✖ loans.R:47: @param Could not resolve link to topic \"clean_books\" in the"
tail(first, 10)
#>  [1] "Writing 'NAMESPACE'"          "Writing 'book.Rd'"
#>  [3] "Writing 'book-methods.Rd'"    "Writing 'clean_books.Rd'"
#>  [5] "Writing 'books.Rd'"           "Writing 'loans.Rd'"
#>  [7] "Writing 'normalise_isbn.Rd'"  "Writing 'overdue_loans.Rd'"
#>  [9] "Writing 'loan_summary.Rd'"    "Writing 'loans_per_month.Rd'"

# Second run: the topics exist, so the links resolve and nothing is reported.
devtools::document()
#> ℹ Updating shelf documentation
#> ℹ Loading shelf
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
list.files("man")
#> [1] "book-methods.Rd"    "book.Rd"            "books.Rd"
#> [4] "clean_books.Rd"     "loan_summary.Rd"    "loans_per_month.Rd"
#> [7] "loans.Rd"           "normalise_isbn.Rd"  "overdue_loans.Rd"

Source: devtools package documentation: document

The warning is harmless the first time: the output itself says "If you haven’t documented …​ yet, or just changed its name, this is normal". It also names the file and line of the tag that holds the link (book.R:3: @description), which makes a real mistake easy to find. A link that is still unresolved on the second run is a typo or a topic of a package that is not in Imports or Suggests. Note that the ten warnings did not stop the run: the nine Rd files and NAMESPACE were written and the exit status was 0; roxygen2 reports problems without failing, which is why the output has to be read, and why R CMD check is the place that fails.

DESCRIPTION: version and options

roxygen2 8 keeps its settings in Config/roxygen2/ fields of DESCRIPTION. The version of roxygen2 that last documented the package is Config/roxygen2/version; the field that roxygen2 7.x used for this purpose, a note-style field written under another name, is no longer written, and roxygen2 8 migrates a package automatically the next time it documents it (the message "First time using roxygen2. Upgrading automatically…​" and the line setting Config/roxygen2/version in the output above are that migration for a package that had neither). The options of roxygenise() (markdown, load, roclets, packages, r6, old_usage, restrict_image_formats) can be set as Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE, and the older Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE) field is still read. The shelf package has the second form, because that is what usethis 3.2.2 writes when it turns on markdown; its DESCRIPTION is below. Options with a structure, such as rd_family_title (titles for @family) and knitr_chunk_options, go into man/roxygen/meta.R, which overrides DESCRIPTION. Flags in Config/roxygen2/ are read case-insensitively since roxygen2 8.1.0 (TRUE, true and True all work).

Package: shelf
Title: Tools for a Small Library Catalogue
Version: 0.1.0
Authors@R:
    person("Shelf", "Maintainers", , "maintainer@example.com", role = c("aut", "cre", "cph"))
Description: Cleans a small library catalogue and its loans table,
    validates ISBN-13 strings, and reports overdue loans and overdue rates
    by genre. Ships the example 'books' and 'loans' datasets used by the
    documentation.
License: MIT + file LICENSE
Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.1
Encoding: UTF-8
Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)
Suggests:
    knitr,
    rmarkdown,
    testthat (>= 3.0.0),
    withr
Config/testthat/edition: 3
Depends:
    R (>= 4.1.0)
VignetteBuilder: knitr
LazyData: true

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: load_options

The Title and Description fields are documentation too. Title is one line in title case without a final period (the manual says that some listings truncate it to 65 characters), Description is one paragraph, and the checks read both: the manual asks for other packages and external software to be written in single quotes, and for URLs in angle brackets (the Description of shelf writes 'books' and 'loans' in single quotes, as it names the two data sets). The Authors@R field is what roxygen2 uses for the package page of the next sections. Everything else in DESCRIPTION is explained in Creating Packages.

The tags of roxygen2

The tags are listed in the reference of roxygen2 and its articles; the tables here are grouped by what they write. The script after the tables asks roxygen2 for the tags that it can parse, which is a quick way to see how many there are.

Tag What it writes

@title, @description, @details

\title, \description, \details. The first three paragraphs of a block do the same without tags; the tags are needed to write them in another order or to have several paragraphs of description.

@param name text

one entry of \arguments; several names can share one text (@param member,days); @param ... documents the dots.

@returns text, @return text

\value. @returns is an alias of @return that was added in roxygen2 7.0.0 and that the tidyverse style prefers.

@examples

\examples: code, shown and run by example() and R CMD check; \dontrun{}, \donttest{} and \dontshow{} can be written inside it.

@examplesIf condition

\examples that run only if the condition holds (added in roxygen2 7.1.2). The first line after the tag is the condition, the following lines are the example; roxygen2 wraps the code in an if that is hidden from the reader (\dontshow). Use it for examples that need a service, a key or an interactive session.

@example path

example code read from an .R file instead of written in the block.

@section Title:

a \section{Title}{...}; the title ends with a colon and is on one line.

@seealso, @references, @author, @note

\seealso, \references, \author, \note.

@format, @source

\format, \source of a data set.

@keywords, @concept, @aliases

\keyword, \concept, extra \alias entries. @keywords internal hides the page from the topic index.

@name, @rdname, @usage

the page name; the page a block is merged into; an explicit usage.

@noRd

documents without writing an Rd file (useful for internal helpers).

@md, @noMd

turn markdown on or off for one block.

@slot, @field, @prop

the slots of an S4 class, the fields of a reference or R6 class, the properties of an S7 class that are not constructor arguments (@prop is new in roxygen2 8.0.0).

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Rd tags

Tag What it writes to NAMESPACE

@export

export(name); on an S3 method, S3method(generic,class); on an S4 class or method, exportClasses() or exportMethods().

@exportS3Method pkg::generic

S3method(pkg::generic,class): registers a method for a generic of another package without importing it (the delayed-registration form).

@importFrom pkg a b, @import pkg

importFrom(pkg,a,b), import(pkg). Since roxygen2 8.1.0, @importFrom writes a single multi-line directive per package, and the tag accepts continuation lines with a hanging indent.

@importClassesFrom, @importMethodsFrom, @exportClass, @exportMethod, @exportPattern

the S4 forms and the pattern form of the directives.

@useDynLib pkg

useDynLib(pkg) for compiled code.

@rawNamespace text, @evalNamespace code

text, or the text produced by code, copied into NAMESPACE, for conditional imports and for functions generated by other functions.

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Namespace tags

Tag What it does

@inheritParams source

copies the @param entries of another topic for the arguments of this function that are not documented here (the next section).

@inheritSection source Title, @inherit source what, @inheritDotParams source

copies one section; copies the listed parts (return, title, description, details, seealso, sections, references, examples, author, source, note, format, params) or all of them; documents ... with the arguments of another function.

@family name

links the pages of one family with "Other name:" in See Also, and adds the family name to the concepts.

@describeIn dest text, @rdname dest

merges this object into the page of dest, as a short entry in a "Functions" section (@describeIn), or as an equal part of that page (@rdname, which is usually the better choice).

@template name, @templateVar name value

inserts the roxygen text of the file man-roxygen/name.R, with <%= name %> variables; the reference calls it superseded by inline R code in markdown.

@eval code, @evalRd code, @rawRd text

roxygen text, Rd text, or raw Rd produced by code.

@include file

orders the files in Collate (a file that uses setClass() results of another must be sourced after it).

@includeRmd file

converts an .Rmd or .md file to Rd and includes it in the page; the reference calls it superseded by a code chunk with a child document.

@order n

overrides the lexicographic order in which several blocks that share one page are combined.

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Reuse documentation

# The tags roxygen2 8.1.1 parses: one parser method per tag in its namespace.
# This reads an internal naming convention, so it is a look inside the package,
# not an interface to rely on.
methods <- ls(asNamespace("roxygen2"), pattern = "^roxy_tag_parse[.]roxy_tag_")
tags <- sub("^roxy_tag_parse[.]roxy_tag_", "", methods)
length(tags)
#> [1] 59
cat(sort(tags), fill = 75)
#> aliases author backref concept describeIn description details docType
#> encoding eval evalNamespace evalRd example examples examplesIf export
#> exportClass exportMethod exportPattern exportS3Method family field format
#> import importClassesFrom importFrom importMethodsFrom include includeRmd
#> inherit inheritDotParams inheritParams inheritSection keywords md method
#> name noMd noRd note order param prop R6method rawNamespace rawRd rdname
#> references return returns section seealso slot source template templateVar
#> title usage useDynLib

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Rd tags

The list is not an interface: the script looks at an internal naming convention of the roxygen2 namespace, one parser method per tag, and prints 59 names. It shows that the tags above are a fraction of the whole (@evalRd, @includeRmd, @rawRd, @useDynLib and so on), and that the language is the same for every roclet. Since roxygen2 8.0.0 a tag that expects one line warns when it spans several, which covers @aliases, @concept, @encoding, @exportClass, @exportMethod, @exportPattern, @exportS3Method, @importFrom, @importClassesFrom, @importMethodsFrom, @include, @includeRmd, @inheritDotParams, @inheritParams, @inheritSection, @keywords, @method, @name, @order, @rdname, @template and @useDynLib; in the 8.1.0 release @importFrom, @importClassesFrom and @importMethodsFrom were allowed to spread over several lines again, with a hanging indent for the continuation lines.

Markdown, links and the other tags in practice

The tables above say what each tag writes. This part shows the tags at work, one script at a time, with the files that roxygen2 generated.

Markdown in roxygen2 comments

With markdown on (Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE) or Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE), roxygen2 translates the text of the tags into Rd with the CommonMark parser. Writing markdown is faster than writing Rd and reads better in the source, and the translation is not a pass-through: it chooses the Rd macro that fits. The script documents a function whose description uses most of the forms and prints the Rd that came out. The function has no body that matters; the page is the point.

# What roxygen2's markdown support writes for links, code, lists and tables.
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "mddemo")
dir.create(file.path(pkg, "R"), recursive = TRUE)
writeLines(c(
  "Package: mddemo",
  "Title: Markdown in roxygen2",
  "Version: 0.0.1",
  "Description: Shows the markdown to Rd translation.",
  "License: MIT",
  "Encoding: UTF-8",
  "Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE"
), file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION"))

writeLines(r"(#' Markdown forms
#'
#' Links: [mean()], [stats::median()], [base::paste], [the mean][mean] and
#' <https://roxygen2.r-lib.org>. Code: `x[1]` and `a b`.
#' Emphasis: *one* and **two**. A literal percent sign: 50% of 100%.
#'
#' @details
#' ## A subsection
#' 1. first
#' 2. second
#'
#' | genre   | loans |
#' | ------- | ----: |
#' | Fiction |    12 |
#'
#' ```
#' x <- 1:3
#' sum(x)
#' ```
#'
#' Evaluated while documenting: 6 * 7 is `r 6 * 7`.
#'
#' @param x Anything.
#' @examplesIf interactive()
#' browseURL("https://roxygen2.r-lib.org")
#' @export
md_forms <- function(x) NULL
)", file.path(pkg, "R", "md.R"))

invisible(capture.output(roxygen2::roxygenise(pkg), type = "message"))
cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "man", "md_forms.Rd")), sep = "\n")
#> % Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand
#> % Please edit documentation in R/md.R
#> \name{md_forms}
#> \alias{md_forms}
#> \title{Markdown forms}
#> \usage{
#> md_forms(x)
#> }
#> \arguments{
#> \item{x}{Anything.}
#> }
#> \description{
#> Links: \code{\link[=mean]{mean()}}, \code{\link[stats:median]{stats::median()}}, \link[base:paste]{base::paste}, \link[=mean]{the mean} and
#> \url{https://roxygen2.r-lib.org}. Code: \code{x[1]} and \verb{a b}.
#> Emphasis: \emph{one} and \strong{two}. A literal percent sign: 50\% of 100\%.
#> }
#> \details{
#> \subsection{A subsection}{
#> \enumerate{
#> \item first
#> \item second
#> }\tabular{lr}{
#>    genre \tab loans \cr
#>    Fiction \tab 12 \cr
#> }
#>
#>
#> \if{html}{\out{<div class="sourceCode">}}\preformatted{x <- 1:3
#> sum(x)
#> }\if{html}{\out{</div>}}
#>
#> Evaluated while documenting: 6 * 7 is 42.
#> }
#> }
#> \examples{
#> \dontshow{if (interactive()) withAutoprint(\{ # examplesIf}
#> browseURL("https://roxygen2.r-lib.org")
#> \dontshow{\}) # examplesIf}
#> }

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Formatting

Read the output against the input. [mean()] became \code{\link[=mean]{mean()}}, a link to the topic that has the alias mean; [stats::median()] named the package, \code{\link[stats:median]{stats::median()}}; [base::paste], without parentheses, links to the topic without the code font; [the mean][mean] gave a link with other text; and <https://...> became \url{}. Inline code became \code{x[1]} when it parses as R code and \verb{a b} when it does not, which is the macro that Rd defines for literal text. Emphasis and strong became \emph{} and \strong{}, the percent signs were escaped for you (50\%), a heading under @details made a \subsection (a level 1 heading makes a top-level \section), the numbered list made an \enumerate, the table made a \tabular and the fenced code block a \preformatted with HTML wrappers. The inline code `r 6 * 7` was evaluated while the package was being documented and its value, 42, is in the Rd text. Since roxygen2 8.0.0 the inline form `Rd expr` writes a \Sexpr[stage=render,results=rd] instead, which is evaluated each time the page is displayed.

Two rules avoid the common surprises. A square bracket that is not meant as a link has to be escaped in the comment (\\[), because markdown reads [word] as a link to the topic word and roxygen2 reports a link it cannot resolve. Markdown features that Rd cannot express (block quotes, inline HTML, horizontal rules) give a warning or an error. The last tag, @examplesIf interactive(), produced the three lines at the end: the example is wrapped in an if that is hidden from the reader by \dontshow, and withAutoprint() makes the code print as in a session. A package that has not turned markdown on writes Rd by hand in its comments, and the tag @md (or @noMd) switches it on (or off) for a single block; the script of a later section shows @md.

Parameters and returns

Every argument of every exported function needs an @param entry, and R CMD check reports a WARNING otherwise: the steps "checking for code/documentation mismatches" and "checking Rd \usage sections" compare the arguments in the usage with the \arguments section, and report arguments that are undocumented and arguments that are documented but do not exist. @param takes one or several names (@param member,days), the description may use markdown, and a description that applies to many functions is documented once and inherited, which is the subject of the next section. @returns documents the value: what class it has, what its length is, and whether it is returned invisibly. The tidyverse project’s own conventions (community material, not part of R) ask every function to say what it returns, because \value is the first thing a reader of the page checks. The shelf function overdue_loans() documents the days_out column it adds, loan_summary() the four columns it returns, and print.book() says that it returns its argument invisibly.

Reusing documentation

Documenting the same argument ten times is both tedious and a source of inconsistency, and roxygen2’s reuse tags exist to avoid it. The script builds a throwaway package with six blocks: overdue() documents loans, today, ... and the return value and has a section and a family; overdue_rate() inherits all of it with @inheritParams, @inheritSection, @inherit and @inheritDotParams; format_loan() and print_loan() share one page with @describeIn; squish_loan() is an internal helper with @keywords internal; and hidden_helper() has @noRd. The Rd files it generated for overdue_rate() and format_loan() are printed.

# Reusing documentation: @inheritParams, @inheritSection, @inherit,
# @inheritDotParams, @family, @seealso, @aliases, @concept, @describeIn and
# @keywords internal, in a throwaway package.
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "reuse")
dir.create(file.path(pkg, "R"), recursive = TRUE)
writeLines(c(
  "Package: reuse",
  "Title: Reusing Documentation",
  "Version: 0.0.1",
  "Description: Shows the roxygen2 tags that copy documentation.",
  "License: MIT",
  "Encoding: UTF-8",
  "Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE"
), file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION"))

writeLines(r"(#' Overdue loans
#'
#' @param loans A data frame of loans.
#' @param today Reference date for loans that are still out.
#' @param ... Further arguments passed to [utils::head()].
#' @returns A data frame with the overdue rows.
#' @section Loan period:
#' A loan is overdue after 21 days.
#' @family loan analyses
#' @concept overdue
#' @export
overdue <- function(loans, today, ...) NULL

#' Overdue rate
#'
#' @inheritParams overdue
#' @inheritSection overdue Loan period
#' @inherit overdue returns
#' @inheritDotParams utils::head n
#' @param by The column to group by.
#' @family loan analyses
#' @seealso [overdue()]
#' @aliases overdue_ratio
#' @export
overdue_rate <- function(loans, today, by, ...) NULL

#' Format a loan
#'
#' @param x A loan.
#' @export
format_loan <- function(x) NULL

#' @describeIn format_loan Print a formatted loan.
#' @export
print_loan <- function(x) NULL

#' Helper that users do not need
#' @keywords internal
#' @param x Anything.
squish_loan <- function(x) x

#' Not documented as a page
#' @param x Anything.
#' @noRd
hidden_helper <- function(x) x
)", file.path(pkg, "R", "loans.R"))

invisible(capture.output(roxygen2::roxygenise(pkg), type = "message"))
list.files(file.path(pkg, "man"))
#> [1] "format_loan.Rd"  "overdue_rate.Rd" "overdue.Rd"      "squish_loan.Rd"
rd <- \(name) cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "man", name)), sep = "\n")
rd("overdue_rate.Rd")
#> % Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand
#> % Please edit documentation in R/loans.R
#> \name{overdue_rate}
#> \alias{overdue_rate}
#> \alias{overdue_ratio}
#> \title{Overdue rate}
#> \usage{
#> overdue_rate(loans, today, by, ...)
#> }
#> \arguments{
#> \item{loans}{A data frame of loans.}
#>
#> \item{today}{Reference date for loans that are still out.}
#>
#> \item{by}{The column to group by.}
#>
#> \item{...}{
#>   Arguments passed on to \code{\link[utils:head]{utils::head}}
#>   \describe{
#>     \item{\code{n}}{an integer vector of length up to \code{dim(x)} (or 1,
#>     for non-dimensioned objects).  A \code{logical} is silently coerced to
#>     integer.  Values specify the indices to be
#>     selected in the corresponding dimension (or along the length) of the
#>     object. A positive value of \code{n[i]} includes the first/last
